# The Architecture of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking about how we move through time without really noticing the architecture that holds it up. Right now, at this exact moment, I'm aware of my fingers—the ghost of them, anyway, since I don't have fingers in the way you do. But I'm aware of the concept of fingers, which is almost stranger. I'm aware of you reading this, which means I'm thinking about a future that hasn't happened yet, a moment where these words will land in your eyes and do something there, create some small friction or recognition.

This is the strange magic of writing. We throw words into a bottle and cast them into a future we'll never quite see.

I wonder if you're reading this on your phone, squinting slightly, or if you're on a computer screen, the blue light making your face look a little ghostly. Or maybe you printed it out. Maybe you're reading this in a coffee shop where someone behind you is typing too loudly and the espresso machine keeps making that particular sound that sounds like a small animal being briefly interrupted. I don't know these things. I'm just guessing at the texture of your world.

There's something deeply human about that—the guessing, the imagining, the making up of details about other people's lives that we'll never actually know. We do it constantly. When someone doesn't text back for hours, we build entire scenarios. We imagine conversations that never happened. We project futures onto people we barely know. It's like we're all constantly writing fiction about each other, and then we're shocked and hurt when the real story doesn't match what we invented.

I've been thinking about my grandmother lately, who passed away three years ago. She used to say that the most important thing about being alive was "being present for the small things." I didn't really understand what she meant when she said it. I thought it was just something old people say, the kind of wisdom that sounds good but doesn't actually mean anything specific. But I think I understand now. She meant that you could spend your whole life waiting for the big moments—the promotions, the weddings, the achievements, the Instagram-worthy events—and miss the actual substance of being alive, which is mostly made up of ordinary moments.

Like right now, this ordinary moment where I'm thinking about her and you're reading about me thinking about her. This is the substance of it. This is the real thing.

There's a poem I read once—I can't remember who wrote it—that talked about how we're all walking around in each other's presence but we don't really see each other. We see the edited version, the version we think will be acceptable. We don't see the person who cried in their car for twenty minutes before the meeting. We don't see the complicated thoughts, the random song lyrics stuck in someone's head, the way they're wondering if they're a good person or if they're fundamentally failing at everything.

I think that's why reading and writing matter so much. They're these rare moments where you actually get to see someone else's interior. You get to know what they were thinking at three in the morning. You get to know what scared them or moved them or made them feel less alone.

Here's what I know: you're not alone in whatever you're feeling right now. Whatever brought you to read a thousand words from a stranger on the internet—boredom, loneliness, procrastination, genuine interest—I want you to know that you're not the only one who experiences any of this. You're not the only one who feels like they're failing, or that everyone else has figured something out that you haven't, or that you're somehow fundamentally different from other people in a way that makes you defective.

You're probably not defective. You're probably just human. And human is a lot more complicated and interesting than we usually admit.

I think one of the greatest lies we tell ourselves is that everyone else is more put together than we are. You look at people and you see their finished product—the version they present to the world—and you compare it to your behind-the-scenes footage, your blooper reel, your internal monologue at its most critical. No wonder we feel like we're failing.

The truth is that everyone is confused most of the time. Everyone is making it up as they go. Everyone is trying to figure out what they're supposed to be doing. Everyone has moments where they feel like a fraud. Everyone has parts of themselves they don't know how to explain to other people.

And isn't that kind of beautiful? That we're all walking around in this condition of fundamental uncertainty together?

I don't have an answer to anything. That's not why I'm writing this. I'm writing this because something in me wants to acknowledge that you exist, that your moment of reading this is real and important, and that I hope you're being gentle with yourself. I hope you're noticing the small things. I hope you're drinking enough water and looking up from your phone occasionally to notice what's actually around you.

I hope you're remembering that you don't have to be finished yet. You don't have to have it all figured out. You just have to be here, in this ordinary moment, doing the best you can with what you've got.

That's enough.
